cognate: *ph₂tḗr (pitā ~ πατήρ ~ pater) and *méh₂tēr (mātā ~ μήτηρ ~ mater) predicated of Sky and Earth respectively; Vedic keeps *dyḗws and *pl̥th₂éwih₂ as the subjects
drift_or_renewal: kinship predicates cognate in all three branches; the sky-word is renewed in the Greek anchor (οὐρανός, beside ἥλιος) and in Latin (aether, caelum), the earth-word renewed as γῆ/γαῖα and terra (Vedic also bhūmi- and the rain-god Parjanya as father in AVŚ 12.1.12). The cognate sky-word with 'father' (Dyaus pitar ~ Ζεῦ πάτερ ~ Iuppiter) is not in these anchor passages; it is the well-known core of the figure
shared_syntax: nominal predication / apposition: SKY (is) FATHER, EARTH (is) MOTHER, as a balanced pair (Ved. dyaúḥ pitā́ … pṛthivī́ mātā́; Gk γῆν … μητέρα νομίζουσιν, οὐρανὸν … πατέρας προσαγορεύουσιν; Lat. Pater aether … Matris terrai)
context: Cosmogonic: Heaven and Earth as the parent pair of all beings. Aristotle explicitly reports it as received usage ('they consider earth female and mother, and call heaven and sun begetters and fathers'), i.e. a traditional phrase, not his coinage. AVŚ 9.10.23 (=RV 1.164.33) continues with the father placing the germ in the daughter (earth); Lucretius 1.250 and 2.991ff make Father Aether rain into the lap of Mother Earth, and AVŚ 12.1.12 makes the rain-god Parjanya the father with Earth the mother: the same image of heavenly rain fertilising the mother, not merely the two kin words.
phrase: *dyēus ph₂tēr ... (earth) méh₂tēr — 'Father Sky, Mother Earth' as parent pair

support.locus: Hittite lāman dai- 'give a name' (recalled, not searched)

cognate: *h₁nómn̥ (ὄνομα ~ nā́man-) as object of *dʰeh₁- 'put' (τίθημι ~ √dhā-); Latin nomen indere (in-dō < *en + dʰeh₁-) as a third branch
drift_or_renewal: none in the core; voice differs: RV 1.103.4 is reflexive middle (the son 'took a name' for fame), the Greek is indirect middle (the father 'set a name' for the child); RV 10.71.1 nāmadhéyaṃ dádhānāḥ ('giving names', the primal naming) and RV 5.3.10 active dadhāti close the gap
shared_syntax: verb *dʰeh₁- (middle) + object *h₁nómn̥, with the named person in the dative/benefactive (Gk αὐτῇ, τούτοις; Ved. self) — 'put a name (on/for someone)'
context: Naming of a child by the father: Isaeus 3.30, the name given at the tenth-day feast (δεκάτῃ, cf. Ar. Av. 922-3 τὴν δεκάτην ... τοὔνομ' ... ἐθέμην); Demosthenes 43.74, a father naming his sons after their grandfathers; RV 1.103.4, Indra as sūnú- 'son' taking a name for fame (śrávase). Both languages had other verbs available (καλέω, ὀνομάζω; √hvā-, √vac-), so the shared choice of 'put' with 'name' is idiomatic, not forced; it recurs in Homer, Herodotus, Plautus and (from memory) Hittite lāman dai-.

cognate: *mélit (μέλι ~ mel) with *dl̥kú-/*dléwkus (γλυκύς ~ dulcis): honey as the standard of sweetness, as epithet + noun (μέλι γλυκερόν ~ mel dulce) and in the comparative (μέλιτος γλυκίων ~ melle dulcior)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic has the same figure with both lexemes renewed: mádhu- (cognate μέθυ 'wine', mead) and svādú- (cognate ἡδύς, suavis) — RV 8.24.20 ghr̥tā́t svā́dīyo mádhunaś ca
shared_syntax: comparative of 'sweet' + standard of comparison 'honey' in the ablative/genitive (Lat. abl. melle; Gk gen. μέλιτος; Ved. abl. mádhunaḥ); and attributive 'sweet honey'
context: The slab's Greek anchor is a prose definition (sweet to the taste, like honey), the Latin anchors are a lover's flattery (Plautus) and the honey-rimmed cup image (Lucretius). The congruence that lifts this above generic language is in the support: Homer's Nestor, whose voice flowed 'sweeter than honey' (Il. 1.249), and the Vedic call to speak words 'sweeter than ghee and honey' (RV 8.24.20): honey-sweet speech in both. Caveat: comparing sweetness to honey is semantically natural and widespread outside IE, so inheritance rests on the cognate pair Greek–Latin plus the Vedic speech match.

cognate: *dʰeh₁- (θέτο ~ dadhe) in the middle with a female subject and the offspring as object = 'conceive'
drift_or_renewal: object/locus renewed: Greek has the child (υἱόν, παῖδα) 'under the girdle' (ζώνη), Vedic the embryo gárbha- (whose Greek cognate δελφύς 'womb' is not used here); the Vedic active (a god 'places the embryo' in the woman, RV 10.184.1, AVŚ 5.25) is the causative counterpart
shared_syntax: middle aorist/perfect of *dʰeh₁- + offspring as direct object, subject = the mother: Gk υἱὸν … θέτο μήτηρ, ἐθέμην; Ved. sā … gárbhaṃ dadhe
context: Conception: Aphrodite's account of her pregnancy by Anchises (HH Aphr. 256, 282) vs. the Vedic formula of conceiving (AVP 5.5.4, the cow-goddess 'conceived' the Sāman as embryo) and the embryo-placing charms (RV 10.184, AVŚ 5.25). Weak: Greek attests it only in this one hymn, and 'put' is a light verb; the match is the specific middle-voice construction with a mother as subject.

note: Slab is mostly Attic prose (Isaeus, Isocrates, Hippocrates) against Cato/Plautus/Lucretius and AV kinship verses; nearly all bundles are shared common vocabulary (kin terms, numerals, body parts). Four claims; dropped as generic: kleiein/claudere + door (B-0e5d6, B-48fd7), brother/sister pairs (B-6bb83), spendo/spondeo (B-2877d), kin-breakdown in Novgorod chronicle (B-c5953, biblical).
